newsitem.title: FRANCE: Chirac, Mandela speak on Zaire crisis.
newsitem.headline: Chirac, Mandela speak on Zaire crisis.

text.p: French and South African presidents Jacques Chirac and Nelson Mandela spoke by telephone on Thursday about Zaire, where both nations favour sending an international force to help refugees threatened by fighting.
French Prime Minister Alain Juppe said "the president spoke to Nelson Mandela, who rang him to talk about the situation in the Great Lakes, Zaire and Rwanda".

Juppe did not elaborate. He was speaking to reporters on the fringes of a Franco-British summit between Chirac and British Prime Minister John Major in the south-western city of Bordeaux, of which Juppe is mayor.
Major told reporters as he arrived in Bordeaux that "there are no doubts about the seriousness of the situation and the need for an international intervention".
"Exactly what, and how? This is among the things we will discuss," he said.
France and Spain this week proposed sending a 5,000-strong multinational force to Zaire to help 1.2 million Hutu refugees threatened by fighting.
The two countries have urged other nations, especially Africans, to help, but have received little response so far.

Mandela has accepted a request from Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko to play a major diplomatic role in peace efforts in central Africa. But it was not clear what he would do to help end fighting in the Great Lakes region, where Zaire's army has been battling ethnic Tutsi rebels supported by Rwanda.

South Africa on Wednesday suspended arms sales to Rwanda and indicated it would contribute troops to an international force for Zaire if asked to do so by the United Nations and the Organisation of African Unity.

The decision to suspend the arms contract followed reports that Rwandan forces were taking part in fighting in eastern Zaire between the region's rival Tutsi and Hutu tribes. The fighting has sparked a flood of refugees out of the area.
